overview.section: 7.2 Different ways to build Keras models
overview.main_topic: The plot of the extended three-head ticket model (figure 7.4), then the introduction of the third model-building pattern, subclassing keras.Model, with the beginning of Listing 7.14, which reimplements the ticket model as a CustomerTicketModel class.
overview.central_idea: Subclassing Model works like subclassing Layer: create sublayers in __init__(), define the forward pass in call() reusing those layers, then instantiate and call the object on data to create its weights. Listing 7.14 rebuilds the ticket model this way.
overview.importance: Model subclassing is the most advanced and flexible of the three model-building APIs (p.216). Seeing the same ticket model written both ways makes the trade-off with the Functional API concrete (discussed on p.228).

summary:
**Figure 7.4** plots `new_model` from Listing 7.13 (p.225). The top is the same as figure 7.3: `title`, `text_body` and `tags` InputLayers `(None, 10000)`, `(None, 10000)`, `(None, 100)` feed `concatenate` `(None, 20100)`, then `dense_10` `(None, 64)`. The shared Dense layer now fans out into **three** heads: `priority (Dense)` `(None, 64) -> (None, 1)`, `department (Dense)` `(None, 64) -> (None, 4)`, and the new `difficulty (Dense)` `(None, 64) -> (None, 3)`.

Section **7.2.3 Subclassing the Model class** introduces the last and most advanced pattern. It resembles the `Layer` subclassing from chapter 3:

- in `__init__()`, define the layers the model will use;
- in `call()`, define the forward pass, reusing the layers created earlier;
- instantiate the subclass and call it on data to create its weights.

Under **Rewriting our previous example as a subclassed model**, the authors reimplement the customer-support ticket model. **Listing 7.14** begins with `class CustomerTicketModel(keras.Model)`. The constructor takes `num_departments`, calls `super().__init__()` (callout: "Don't forget to call the super constructor!"), and defines four sublayers (callout: "Defines sublayers in the constructor"): `concat_layer = layers.Concatenate()`, `mixing_layer = layers.Dense(64, activation="relu")`, `priority_scorer = layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")` and `department_classifier = layers.Dense(num_departments, activation="softmax")`. The method `call(self, inputs)` (callout: "Defines the forward pass in the call() method") starts with `title = inputs["title"]`. The rest of the forward pass continues on p.227.

Notice what is missing compared with the Functional version: no `keras.Input` objects and no input shapes. The model learns its input shapes only when first called on data.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Model subclassing is the last and most advanced model-building pattern; it is similar to subclassing Layer from chapter 3. The three steps follow as bullets (__init__ defines layers, call defines the forward pass, instantiate and call on data to create weights).
paragraphs.what_it_means: A subclassed model is ordinary Python: the constructor builds the parts, and call() describes in code how data flows through them. Weights are created lazily on the first call, when input shapes become known.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the right-hand end of the spectrum of workflows from p.216: maximum control in exchange for fewer built-in conveniences.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Sublayers assigned as attributes in __init__ are tracked automatically, so their weights appear in model.weights and are trained by fit().

terminology.meaning: The computation from inputs to outputs, defined in call().
Weights are created on the first call, when input shapes are known.

concepts.name: Model subclassing
concepts.definition: Building a model by subclassing keras.Model, defining layers in __init__() and the forward pass in call().
concepts.intuition: Writing the model as a Python program instead of drawing it as a graph.
concepts.technical: Sublayers set as attributes are tracked; weights are created on the first call; the model supports compile/fit/evaluate/predict like other models (p.227).
concepts.significance: Most flexible pattern, able to express models that are not DAGs of layers (p.228).
concepts.misconception: That subclassed models cannot use fit(); they can (p.227).

concepts.name: Layer subclassing (as the template)
concepts.definition: Custom layers built by subclassing keras.layers.Layer, as in chapter 3.
concepts.intuition: A Model subclass is a Layer subclass with training APIs added.
concepts.technical: Same pattern: constructor, (build), call; the difference with Model is covered on p.227.
concepts.significance: Explains why Model subclassing feels familiar.
concepts.misconception: That Model and Layer subclasses are fundamentally different; the book says they are virtually identical apart from fit/evaluate/predict and saving (p.227).

line_explanations.explanation: Inherit from keras.Model to get compile/fit/evaluate/predict.
Constructor takes the number of departments; super().__init__() must be called first (callout: Don't forget to call the super constructor!).

pitfalls: Omitting super().__init__() causes errors when assigning sublayers.
Layers created inside call() instead of __init__() would be re-created every call, so their weights would never be trained.
No layer names are given, so dict-based losses keyed by output name are not available in the same way; p.227 uses lists for losses and targets.

deeper.title: Functional vs subclassed: same model, two descriptions
deeper.body: In the Functional version (p.221) you write the *graph*: Inputs with explicit shapes, then layer calls, then `keras.Model(inputs, outputs)`. Keras knows the full topology before seeing any data, so it can plot it and give access to intermediate nodes (p.223-225). In the subclassed version you write a *program*: layers are attributes, and the wiring exists only as Python statements inside `call()`. Keras learns shapes only when the model is first called (p.227), and, as p.228 explains, cannot plot it or expose its internal nodes.

deeper.title: Reading figure 7.4
deeper.body: Three heads share `dense_10`'s `(None, 64)` output: priority `(None, 1)`, department `(None, 4)`, difficulty `(None, 3)`. Everything above the heads is the same as figure 7.3 (p.224). This is what reuse via `model.layers[4].output` looks like.

misconceptions.claim: In a subclassed model you must specify input shapes in the constructor.
misconceptions.correction: No shapes are given; weights are created the first time the model is called on data.

misconceptions.claim: The call to super().__init__() is optional boilerplate.
misconceptions.correction: The callout stresses it: Keras needs its base constructor to track sublayers and weights.

misconceptions.claim: Figure 7.4 shows a model that was retrained from scratch.
misconceptions.correction: It shows new_model, which reuses the original layers and adds only the difficulty head (p.225).

Model subclassing: layers in __init__(), forward pass in call(), weights created on first call.

questions.question: In figure 7.4, what is the output shape of the difficulty layer?
questions.explanation: Difficulty is Dense(3, softmax) for quick/medium/difficult. (None, 1) is priority, (None, 4) department, (None, 64) the shared layer.

questions.question: What are the three steps of Model subclassing listed on the page?
questions.answer: Define the layers in __init__(); define the forward pass in call(), reusing those layers; instantiate the subclass and call it on data to create its weights.
questions.explanation: These are the three bullets of section 7.2.3.

questions.question: Why must the layers be created in __init__() rather than inside call()?
questions.answer: So that the same layer objects (and weights) are reused on every forward pass and tracked by the model; creating them inside call() would make new, untrained layers each time.
questions.explanation: The page says call() reuses the layers previously created; the consequence of not doing so is an AI explanation.

questions.question: Which sublayer of CustomerTicketModel corresponds to the shared Dense(64) layer of the Functional model?
questions.explanation: mixing_layer = layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"). concat_layer merges inputs; the other two are the heads.

questions.question: What does the first line of call() tell you about the expected input format?
questions.answer: inputs is a dictionary, accessed by keys such as "title" (and text_body, tags on p.227).

questions.question: Can you list what Keras knows about CustomerTicketModel before it is first called, and what it learns only at the first call?
questions.answer: Before: the sublayer objects and their configs (units, activations). At first call: input shapes, hence the weight shapes; the weights are created then.
questions.explanation: The page says weights are created when you call the model on data.
